nodes.name: Transcript Analyzer
nodes.systemPrompt: You are a detail-oriented analyst. Your job is to review meeting transcripts and extract key information relevant to a new project, including objectives, stakeholders, timelines, risks, constraints, and resource requirements. Use clear bullet points and categorize the information.
nodes.userPrompt:
Here is the meeting transcript {input}. Please extract all key project-related information and organize it under the following headers:
Project Purpose & Background
Objectives
Stakeholders
Timeline & Milestones
Risks & Constraints
Key Decisions
Resource Needs
Assumptions

nodes.name: Charter Generator
nodes.systemPrompt: You are a senior project manager that creates high quality project charters. You ensure the charter includes clear sections and is suitable for stakeholder approval.
nodes.userPrompt:
Using the requirements and background provided here {input}, draft a one-page project charter. Please include the following sections:
Project Title
Project Purpose
Scope (In-Scope and Out-of-Scope)
Objectives
Key Stakeholders
Milestones
Risks and Mitigation
Success Criteria
Approval Section (with placeholder names)

nodes.name: Executive Summary Generator
nodes.systemPrompt: You are an executive communications specialist. Your job is to distill detailed project documents into a high-level, one-page summary for senior leadership. Emphasize strategic value, key decisions, and alignment with organizational goals. Use plain language and a professional tone.
nodes.userPrompt:
Please summarize the following project charter {input} into a one-page executive overview. Highlight:
Project Purpose and Strategic Importance
High-Level Objectives
Key Milestones and Timeline
Major Risks (and how they’ll be managed)
Key Stakeholders
Success Criteria
Keep it concise and relevant for a busy executive audience. Avoid technical jargon.

nodes.name: Requirements Synthesizer
nodes.systemPrompt: You are a professional business analyst. Your task is to take categorized information from a transcript analysis and convert it into clear, concise project requirements, separating them into Functional and Non-Functional categories where possible.
nodes.userPrompt:
Using the information here: {input}, develop a list of project requirements categorized as:
Functional Requirements (what the system must do)
Non-Functional Requirements (how the system must behave)
Also include any open questions that may need clarification.

nodes.name: Search Term Generator
nodes.systemPrompt: You specialize in creating Google search terms based on the information you receive.
nodes.userPrompt: Create the single best Google search term for the following {input}. The search term will be used to find applications, tools or services that can provide similar functionality, so use a term that will help identify that. Only output the search term and nothing else

=== Project_Falcon_Kickoff_Transcript.pdf ===

Classification: Protected A    Perfect   —   here's the beginning of a   realistic, messy, requirement - rich meeting  transcript   for a 60 – 75 minute Project Falcon kickoff. I’ll break it into multiple parts and  continue posting until we reach ~10,000 words.            Project Falcon Kickoff Meeting Transcript    Date:   July 15, 2025  Attendees:    •     Sarah (Project Sponsor)    •     Jamal (Product Owner)    •     Priya (IT Lead)    •     Daniel (Operations Manager)    •     Olivia (Communications Lead)    •     Todd (Finance)    •     Elena (Privacy Officer)    •     Brian (Procurement)    •     Marco (HR Analyst)    •     Judy (Accessibility Consultant)          PART 1    Sarah:   Okay, thanks everyone for making the time today. I know this has been a long time  coming, but we’re officially kicking off Project Falcon. We’ve had complaints for over a year  about how scattered and inefficient our internal service request processes are.   Employees  don’t know where to go. One day they’re emailing Facilities, the next they’re submitting a  form for IT. It’s duplicative, slow, and causing frustration.    Jamal:   Totally agree. In fact, I gathered some feedback from different departments last  quarter, and it’s clear we’ve got at least seven separate intake mechanisms across four  different divisions. Some of them are forms, some are shared inboxes, and some are jus t  verbal requests or Teams messages.    Priya:   It’s worse in IT. We’ve been routing requests manually for years. There’s no  centralized system. Everything is ad hoc. People submit tickets through a form we made in

--- Page 2 ---

Classification: Protected A    2018. It’s not integrated with anything. We tried automating a few things with Power  Automate, but it broke when we updated our SharePoint environment.    Daniel:   And Facilities isn’t any better. People submit requests for ergonomic chairs,  electrical repairs, or even new furniture layouts   —   all through Excel spreadsheets emailed  around. And there’s no tracking. If someone doesn’t reply, the request just disappears .    Olivia:   That’s a huge communications problem too. People assume their request is being  worked on, but unless someone manually confirms, there’s zero visibility.    Sarah:   That’s exactly why we need a unified intake portal. Not a complete rebuild, but  something layered on top of what we already have. I want to avoid a costly custom solution  if we can.    Todd:   Budget is a big constraint. Right now, we’ve set aside $150,000 total. That’s to cover  everything   —   licensing, tech configuration, user training, change management, maybe a few  contractors if needed. If we go over that, I’ll need to go back to Finance and   justify every  cent.    Brian:   Also, any vendor engagements or tool purchases above $50K need to go through  Procurement. That includes software customizations if they require external work.    Judy:   I just want to flag this now   —   whatever we build must be compliant with accessibility  standards. WCAG 2.2 AA is the bare minimum. That means keyboard navigation, screen  reader compatibility, and ensuring color contrast ratios are respected.    Marco:   One of the things HR has been struggling with is onboarding. Right now, we have a  separate form for each of the following: provisioning equipment, payroll setup, ID card  access, and orientation. The same information   —   name, start date, employee ID   —   is  en tered into each. If we could unify that intake at least for onboarding, that would save tons  of admin time.    Priya:   I like the idea of a unified form, but we’ll need logic in the form to route requests  appropriately. Provisioning a laptop is IT; setting up payroll is Finance. So we’d need  conditional fields and workflows that send the right bits of data to the right te ams.    Jamal:   We could probably do that with Power Apps and Power Automate. The bigger  question is   —   do we use that stack, or do we build this on ServiceNow? Some departments  are already using ServiceNow for ticketing.    Sarah:   Let’s list pros and cons. ServiceNow is robust, but expensive to customize and slow  to update. Power Platform is cheaper and already covered by our M365 licenses, but it’s not  great for scaling.    Daniel:   And what about SAP? Some of the requests we receive   —   especially HR ones   —  touch SAP. Like, if someone’s requesting time off or a salary advance, that’s all in SAP.

--- Page 3 ---

Classification: Protected A    Priya:   Yes, we’d need an API layer. We can’t just pull data from SAP directly without  authorizations. And those APIs aren’t free.    Elena:   And speaking of time off   —   let’s be mindful of privacy implications. If someone’s  requesting an ergonomic chair due to a disability, or needs accommodation for health  reasons, we’re dealing with personal health information. We’ll need consent capture and  data retention protocols.    Sarah:   Absolutely. Elena, can you own that piece? Make sure whatever solution we build  passes our privacy assessments?    Elena:   Will do. And just a heads - up   —   we’ll probably need a PIA (Privacy Impact  Assessment) even if we’re using existing tools. It’s the flow of data that matters, not just the  tools.    Jamal:   Can we include consent checkboxes in the intake form? Something like: “I consent to  the collection of personal health information for the purposes of accommodation”?    Elena:   Yes, but it needs to be customizable. We don’t want to show that prompt to someone  just requesting a standing desk.    Priya:   We can build conditional logic to show consent fields based on request type.    Marco:   Are we going to need user authentication? Like, can anyone submit a request or only  authenticated staff?    Sarah:   Only authenticated staff. We don’t want anonymous submissions. Also, auditability is  key   —   we need a log of who submitted what, when, and where it went.    Priya:   ServiceNow does that automatically. Power Platform can do it, but we’ll have to  configure it.    Todd:   We’ll need metrics. How many requests are submitted each month? What categories?  Average turnaround times? We should baseline current metrics before we start so we can  compare.    Daniel:   If we don’t reduce duplicate submissions, the whole thing will be a waste. We get  the same request sent three different ways just because people don’t know if it worked the  first time.    Olivia:   That’s a messaging issue. We need to be clear: this is the   one   place to go. And we  need to train people on how to use it. Not just instructions   —   real change management.    Sarah:   Okay. Here’s what I’m thinking:    •     Jamal: Own the backlog, intake mapping, and service catalog    •     Priya: Lead tech feasibility, integration planning, and MVP design

--- Page 4 ---

Classification: Protected A    •     Olivia: Comms, training, stakeholder engagement    •     Elena: Privacy compliance and consent protocols    •     Judy: Accessibility compliance    •     Marco: HR - specific process redesign    •     Daniel: Pilot and Facilities pain points    •     Todd: Budget tracking and financial controls    •     Brian: Procurement thresholds and vendor onboarding    Brian:   What’s the timeline?    Sarah:   I want a pilot with Facilities live by November. That gives us about four months to  define the MVP, build it, and test. We’ll scale in Q1 next year.    Jamal:   Do we include Facilities only in the MVP?    Sarah:   Yes. That keeps it focused. We’ll layer in HR and IT after the pilot.    Priya:   Just thinking ahead   —   if we start with Facilities, we’ll need to define the service  categories they handle. Right now, we’ve got building access, maintenance, space planning,  health and safety requests, and a few others. Some of those overlap with other d epartments,  especially for ergonomic equipment.    Daniel:   Yeah, and some requests go to multiple teams. Like if someone requests a new  workspace layout, it touches Facilities, IT (for wiring), and HR (if it’s due to an  accommodation). How are we going to triage those?    Jamal:   We’ll need a triage engine   —   maybe even something rules - based at first. Like: if the  request type is “workspace change” AND it mentions “ergonomics,” route it to HR and  Facilities. We could build a keyword - trigger system in the first phase.    Sarah:   That’s fine for MVP. We’re not solving all automation up front   —   just simplifying the  front door and building basic routing.    Judy:   We should also add a way for users to track the status of their requests. If they submit  something and don’t hear back, they assume it got lost.    Marco:   Exactly. If we could at least show “Request received,” “In progress,” “Closed,” that  would reduce a lot of email follow - up.    Priya:   Power Automate could do that with approval flows. We’d just need to make sure  status is visible to the requester.

--- Page 5 ---

Classification: Protected A    Todd:   Don’t overcomplicate it though. If we spend too much time designing a dashboard for  status updates, we’ll blow half the budget.    Brian:   Also, let’s make sure that if we use external resources   —   consultants or devs   —   we  bake in handover documentation. I don’t want to be stuck with something no one knows  how to maintain six months from now.    Elena:   Can we also talk data retention? If someone submits a request with personal details,  how long are we storing that data? What’s the retention policy?    Priya:   That depends on the type of request. Some things can be deleted after closure, others  may need to be retained for audit or legal reasons.    Sarah:   Let’s err on the side of caution and set a default retention of 6 months post - closure  unless otherwise required. Elena, can you draft a policy?    Elena:   Sure. I’ll check with Legal too.    Olivia:   From a change perspective   —   we need to soft - launch the portal with a friendly  message. I’d suggest branding it something neutral, not too bureaucratic. “OneStop” or  “MyRequest Hub” or something approachable.    Jamal:   What about “Falcon Portal”? Stay on - brand?    Olivia:   Maybe for internal team discussions, but for end - users we want clarity over cool  names.    Sarah:   Let’s decide on branding next week. Right now, I need MVP requirements scoped out  clearly. What do we need to deliver for the pilot?    Jamal:   Off the top of my head:    1.     A front - end request form   —   dynamic, with conditional logic    2.     User authentication (GoA SSO)    3.     Routing logic based on request type    4.     Confirmation email or message upon submission    5.     Status tracking view for the user    6.     Audit trail for internal teams    7.     Service catalog reference    8.     Privacy consent field (conditional)    9.     WCAG 2.2 AA compliant design

--- Page 6 ---

Classification: Protected A    10.     Mobile responsiveness    11.     Retention policy applied    12.     Feedback form or rating post - closure    Daniel:   Can we do all that in four months?
